faq.a: Stomach juice is very acidic, usually around pH 1.5 to 3.5, because the lining makes hydrochloric acid. That is strong enough to kill most germs and to switch on the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin.

faq.q: What does the mucus in the stomach do?
faq.a: A thick gel of mucus coats the stomach lining. It slows acid and enzymes from reaching the cells and holds a protective layer of bicarbonate against the wall.
asks: Tell me about the thick mucus coat

faq.a: Bicarbonate is an alkaline chemical, like the baking soda in a kitchen. Stomach lining cells release it into the mucus, where it neutralises acid before it reaches them.
asks: Tell me about the bicarbonate shield

faq.q: Why does the stomach make acid at all?
faq.a: The acid kills most germs in food, helps unfold proteins, and turns on pepsin, an enzyme that chops proteins into smaller pieces.
asks: What does stomach acid do to food?

faq.q: How fast does the stomach lining renew?
faq.a: The surface cells of the stomach lining are replaced every few days, so small areas of wear are quickly repaired.
asks: Does the stomach replace its lining?

facts: Stomach acid is mostly hydrochloric acid, made by parietal cells in the stomach lining.
Stomach juice usually has a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5.
The surface cells of the stomach lining are renewed every few days.
